A checkup was a minor medical examination conducted periodically on human children and adults by a certified health practitioner for basic medical observation and preventive health purposes.

## Overview Edit

If a child or adult was sick or injured, however, a medical practitioner of higher skill and capability would conduct a more extensive test in the form of an examination. A check-up was generally designed to catch more easily remedied ailments before they became too serious, and involved a general evaluation of the patient's body and a check to ensure that all of their bodily systems were healthy for their age group. ^{[1]}

In the United Kingdom in the present day, the National Health Service recommended a patient undergo a check-up annually after the age of 50 for their general health, or on an ad-hoc basis if their health was compromised. ^{[2]}

The Gideon Sensor is one of many Sensors in the game Dead Space. It records the sounds of nearby creatures and translates them to readable symbols on a scanner. It's equipped with a motion meter which gives a general estimation of the location of Isaac and his foes. The user has two options to interact with the sensor. The user can either press left or right to rotate the image, or press up to raise the scanner. The latter can also be pressed over and over, indefinitely, which will cause the scanner's pitch and the motion meter to get higher. It becomes harder to read the scanner with a higher pitch, but it's possible to hear the movement of Isaac's and the enemy's movements.

The secretive, solitary Monster. They seem to appear out of nowhere and just as soon leave as they arrive: sometimes disappearing for the whole winter. They are usually loners.

Animalia, and sometimes other life forms, fall under this category as well; a monster is sometimes defined by its appearance or reputation alone, and is frequently misunderstood or feared more than it should.

Of course, this may be for good reason, as sometimes monsters are villains. A monster may be humanoid and have supernatural qualities, or it may be completely animal-like (thus the connection to lycanthropes). In the case that monsters possess both human and animal features, the character that has both is usually referred to as a Were-creature.

This study investigated differences in responses to false questioning/beliefs from six family caregivers supporting people with dementia. The false statements and questions produced by participants were audio-recorded and transcribed for analysis. To describe the prevalence of lying to people with dementia and to assess attitudes associated with lying to the person with dementia.

## Research questions:

- Does the use of lying as a strategy to manage challenging behavior change with dementia occur?
- What factors are associated with lying to people with dementia?

## Key findings:

- One in three study participants reported using lying when communicating with or caring for persons with dementia.
- The use of lying was more likely with persons with a diagnosis of dementia that was less than five years old.
- Caregivers were also shown to be less likely to use lying to people with dementia compared with nursing professionals.

## Introduction

Communicating and interacting with a person with dementia can be challenging as the person is no longer able to make sense of their world because of cognitive decline. Being a communicator does however not solely depend on talking. For people with dementia a simple smile or listening to the person is often more appreciated than talking itself.

Being attentive and non-judgmental enables us to be a receptive communicator of care. Attunement, reflective listening and active listening are some of the ways we can communicate with those with dementia.

## Understanding the person

In order to be attuned to those for whom we provide care and support, it is important to understand their dementia; that is, to appreciate the way their environment and their world is affected and changing for them.

We must never assume that we know how people are feeling inside but try to understand them and their experiences through their actions and behaviours. If we are able to identify and understand the cause of the distress a dementia sufferer is experiencing, we are then able to find ways to alleviate it.

For the most part, if harm is inflicted (i.e. a lie causes or allows someone to take an action that leads to harm or suffering), that is unethical. The Delphi technique is a multistage process involving a series of questionnaire rounds, interspersed by controlled feedback based on the results of previous rounds that seek to gain the most reliable consensus of opinion of a group of experts (Linstone & Turoff, 1975; Gordon & Pease, 2005; Vernon, 2009). It involves progressive rounds of survey construction, analysis and iterative revision until predefined criteria for consensus are reached. Participants receive feedback on responses to previous rounds and can use this feedback to inform their decisions about future survey responses and the process continues until there is emergence of consensus (Gordon & Pease 2006; Vernon 2009). Delphi studies commonly comprise three rounds before consensus is achieved (Hasson et al. 2000; Hanafin & Brooks 2005). Information on the topic under investigation may be derived from alternative sources obtained prior to the first round of the Delphi and this can inform initial survey content and structural features (Landeta 2006).

There are four aspects to Delphi survey methodology (Delbecq et al. 1975, Munro et al. 1996, Pajares & Valiante 2000). There are an initial survey of a group of experts, usually via a questionnaire, to assess the range of expertise and obtain a preliminary result. The results of the survey are returned to all stakeholders, often with added commentary to assist in further understanding of data gathered. Data gathered from the first round of the Delphi survey is then used to make refinements to the survey questions. Anonymity is maintained to all survey participants unless disclosure is specifically required by the participants themselves. The second round of the survey then occurs, again usually by questionnaire, with the questions changed due to the feedback of the previous round.

## Introduction

Communicating and interacting with a person with dementia can be challenging as the person is no longer able to make sense of their world because of cognitive decline. Being a communicator does however not solely depend on talking. For people with dementia a simple smile or listening to the person is often more appreciated than talking itself.

Being attentive and non-judgmental enables us to be a receptive communicator of care. Attunement, reflective listening and active listening are some of the ways we can communicate with those with dementia.

## Understanding the person

In order to be attuned to those for whom we provide care and support, it is important to understand their dementia; that is, to appreciate the way their environment and their world is affected and changing for them.

We must never assume that we know how people are feeling inside but try to understand them and their experiences through their actions and behaviours. If we are able to identify and understand the cause of the distress a dementia sufferer is experiencing, we are then able to find ways to alleviate it.
